reviewed.by: ROUND 2 — fixes applied from apologia-argument (2 BREAK, 2 WEAK, 5 POLISH) and apologia-citations (1 ERROR, 8 CHECK). NOT YET RE-GATED; orthodoxy has never run. STANDING CONSTRAINTS, do not undo: (1) The CLOSE must not argue about date or authorship. The original close, 'details no forger would think to invent', was a claim about authorship and it contradicted the scope bound 12 seconds earlier; it is also invalid against the actual critical position, which is a LATE AUTHOR WITH ACCESS TO BABYLONIAN MEMORY, not an inventor. Daniel's date also divides orthodox Christians, so a date claim forfeits denominational neutrality. The close now uses the essay's own final sentence. (2) The hedge belongs on the RENDERING of Daniel 5:16/5:7, not on the downstream inference: the essay's stamp records a prior argument gate adding 'on the likely sense of Dan 5:16' and flagging it [contested rendering] -- Montgomery reads taltiy as an OFFICE title (Akkadian shalshu, 'thirdling'/triumvir), which would dissolve the whole payoff. Round 1 moved that hedge onto the inference and upgraded 'a natural reading' to 'the natural reading'. Do not re-harden it. (3) 'An earlier generation of critics' -- the essay's own words. No serious critic has used Belshazzar against Daniel since Dougherty 1929; the modern late-date case rests on the Greek loanwords, the Aramaic dialect, placement in the Ketuvim, and Daniel 11. Undated 'critics' misrepresents an abandoned position as a live one. (4) Belshazzar was ONE of the alleged blunders, never 'the giveaway' -- Darius the Mede is the one specialists call the book's hardest historical problem. (5) Keep 'not by itself' / 'on its own' in the scope bound: the essay says 'though not by itself the book's date', which leaves room for the cumulative case. (6) Never say archaeology 'proves the Bible' (the essay's opening calls that leap a mistake), and never say no find has ever contradicted a biblical claim (retired 2026-07-28; NOTE: that claim has NO entry in tools/retired-claims.json, so nothing catches it mechanically -- add one). (7) Do not claim critics doubted Pontius Pilate's existence; he is attested by Tacitus, Josephus and Philo. (8) Scene 14 is the man-and-authority bound; scene 15 is the archaeology-does-not-prove bound; scene 16 is the close. (Round 1's note had these numbers off by one.)

voiceover: For a long time, one name in the Bible had no evidence outside it. Daniel chapter five tells of a feast in Babylon, a hand writing on the wall, and a king named Belshazzar. The problem was that no source outside the Bible knew him. The Babylonian king lists ended the dynasty with a king called Nabonidus. The classical historians agreed. There was no Belshazzar in the Babylonian records. So an earlier generation of critics concluded: the author of Daniel did not know Babylon. He had got Babylon's kings wrong. It was treated as one of the telltale blunders — a mistake showing the book was written late, by someone far from the events. Then the cuneiform was read. A cylinder of Nabonidus names his eldest son. Bel-shar-usur. Belshazzar. And the Babylonian records say something stranger still. For years Nabonidus was not even in Babylon. He was at Tema, in Arabia, and he entrusted the kingship to his son. So Belshazzar was real, and he was ruling — but the crown was his father's. He was second, and he stayed second. Now go back to Daniel five. Belshazzar offers a reward to anyone who can read the writing. And what he offers is oddly specific: to be made the third ruler in the kingdom. Not second. Third. On the likely sense of the Aramaic, that is because the first two places were already taken — by Nabonidus, and by Belshazzar himself. An odd detail turns out to fit a political arrangement lost until the tablets were read. Be careful what this does and does not show. It establishes the man and his authority. It does not, on its own, settle when Daniel was written, or the events it narrates. Archaeology does not prove the Bible, and anyone who tells you it does is overselling. What it does is this: on detail after detail, it shows the writers knew their world. And a source that reliable deserves to be weighed, not waved away.
